newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says no retreat on Framatome conditions.
newsitem.headline: France says no retreat on Framatome conditions.

text.p: The French government repeated on Wednesday it would not retreat on terms it has set for allowing the proposed merger of state-controlled nuclear giant Framatome with Anglo-French engineering group GEC-Alsthom.
Industry Minister Franck Borotra told the national assembly the five conditions -- which include French interests keeping a majority stake in the enlarged industrial group -- "are not negotiable."
He gave no hint about progress in talks on the merger that would create the world's second largest power engineering group, saying only they were under way and that there was no deadline.
"We face no time constraints on the subject," he said in response to questions.

Alcatel Alsthom and Britain's General Electric Co announced last August plans to study a merger between their 50-50 joint venture company GEC-Alsthom and Framatome, the world's biggest maker of nuclear power plants.

Aside from retaining control of strategic nuclear decisions, other conditions involve continuing Franco-German cooperation on the future EPR power station, preservation of the identity of Framatome's nuclear activities, the predominance of French interest in the new combination and provision for nuclear risks.
"France will keep control over its nuclear activites." he said.
Borotra underlined that Framatome would stick to its agreement with German engineering firm Siemens"in all its elements."
In 1989, Framatome formed a joint venture with Siemens to develop a reactor -- called a European pressurised water reactor (EPR) -- for France and Germany and for export.

The government will not authorise the operation "if there is no shareholders' pact between the public sector and the French company Alcatel Alsthom which will have a stake at least equal that of a foreign partner," Borotra said.
Alcatel Alsthom, which owns 44 percent of Framatome, recently reached an agreement with other shareholders to retain majority French control if GEC takes an interest.
Last month, GEC chairman Lord Weinstock was quoted as saying he wanted at least 50 percent of the new group.
Borotra said the government was aiming to "build a French capital-based electrical engineering group on a world scale."
